title: Oneness, explained
hookLine: one common way to explain it: one Lord, alone worshiped, with names and attributes unlike any other

lines: SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE!
cards: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" A short surah, only a few lines in Pickthall's English. Sahih al-Bukhari records a man who heard another recite it over and over through the night.
In the morning he told the Prophet about it, as if he thought it too little. The answer: by the One in whose hand my soul is, it equals a third of the Qur'an. A third, from a few short lines.
Whatever they say about oneness must run deep.

teach.b: Tawhid. Making one, affirming oneness. It's the idea under la ilaha illallah.
One common way to explain it splits it into three parts, so you can see oneness from three sides. First, one Lord.
The opening surah says: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." One who creates, sustains and runs everything.
Plenty of people, the Qur'an says, would agree with that much: ask who made the heavens and the earth, and they will say Allah.
Second, one alone worshiped. This is the side the shahadah presses hardest. Acknowledging one Creator, then still bowing to other things, isn't tawhid in this sense.
Prayer, trust, deepest fear and hope all go one way. Third, names and attributes unlike any other. Allah is called the Merciful, the Hearer, the Seer.
People hear and see too, so how is that different?
The Qur'an answers in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." The names are real, and nothing is like the one they name.
The surah of oneness closes: "And there is none comparable unto Him." That three-part way isn't the only one.
Other schools of Muslim theology explain oneness under different headings, and later this year has days for them.
But the three sides make a simple frame to hold: one in who rules, one in who is worshiped, one in what He is like.

how: Muslims learn tawhid in early religious lessons, often through Surah al-Ikhlas (112), which can be recited in the daily prayers; some schools teach it in three parts, lordship, worship, and names and attributes, while others use different theological headings.

o: unity among Muslims, all praying as one community
oneness: one Lord, one alone worshiped, none like Him
the single direction all Muslims face to pray

p: prayer and trust go one way
equals a third of the Qur'an

s: the three-part explanation is the only way Muslims explain tawhid
it's one common way; other schools of theology use different headings.
the Qur'an says nothing is like Him, yet calls Him the Hearer, the Seer
"Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer."
believing in one Creator is all tawhid asks
in this explanation, worship going to Him alone is a side of its own.

games.q: a man recites the short surah of oneness again and again through the night. someone thinks it's too little and tells the Prophet. what does he say?
o: he should recite a longer surah.
it equals a third of the Qur'an.
games.why: Sahih al-Bukhari records it: a few short lines on oneness, weighed as a third of the Qur'an.

practice: Choose one side and stay with it: for one Lord, rest your attention on something you didn't make and can't keep running, your heartbeat, the weather, the light; for one worshiped, ask quietly where your trust goes when things go wrong; for names unlike any other, take one word, merciful, and notice how far any mercy you've known falls short of it.
If you pray, you can recite the surah of oneness.

wordCard.voice: Tawhid. Oneness: one Lord, one alone worshiped, and names nothing else can share. Today's word.

orig.note: making one, affirming the oneness of God.

carryVoice: Your line: one in every way. Three sides of a single idea. Until tomorrow.
